delta.definition: How much the option's price moves when the underlying moves $1. A delta of 0.50 gains about $0.50 per $1 rise. Calls have positive delta, puts negative. Also a rough guide to the odds of finishing in the money.

gamma.definition: How fast delta itself changes as the underlying moves. High gamma means your exposure shifts quickly, typical of at-the-money options close to expiry.

theta.definition: Time decay: how much value the option loses per day if nothing else changes. Negative for buyers (time works against you), positive for writers.

vega.definition: How much the option's price changes when implied volatility moves one percentage point. Long options gain when volatility rises; short options lose.

iv.definition: The market's expectation of how much the underlying will swing, per year, backed out of option prices. Higher IV means more expensive options.

premium.definition: The price of an option. Buyers pay it up front; writers (sellers) receive it.

strike.definition: The price at which the option settles. A call pays out above its strike at expiry, a put pays out below it.

expiry.definition: When the option settles. Zenith options are European: they can only be exercised at expiry, settled against the oracle price.

call.definition: The right to the upside above the strike. Buying a call is a bet the price rises; selling one means you pay out if it does.

put.definition: The right to the downside below the strike. Buying a put is a bet the price falls (or a hedge); selling one means you pay out if it does.

bid.definition: The price you receive if you write (sell) this option right now. Click a bid to sell.

ask.definition: The price you pay to buy this option right now. Click an ask to buy.

oi.definition: How many contracts of this option are currently open. A rough measure of liquidity and interest.

volume.definition: How many contracts of this option traded recently.

itm.definition: An option that would pay out if it expired right now: a call with the strike below spot, or a put with the strike above spot. Shaded in the chain.

atm.definition: The strike closest to the current spot price. ATM options have the most time value and the highest gamma.

spot.definition: The current market price of the underlying asset.

collateral.definition: Balance locked when you write an option, so the payout is guaranteed if it finishes in the money: 100% of spot for calls, 110% of the strike for puts. Released when you close.

breakeven.definition: The underlying price at expiry where the trade neither makes nor loses money, after the premium.

max-loss.definition: The most the position can lose at expiry. Buying options caps it at the premium paid; writing uncovered calls has no cap.

net-debit.definition: A multi-leg trade that costs money to open: you pay more premium than you receive.

net-credit.definition: A multi-leg trade that pays you to open: you receive more premium than you pay.

long.definition: You bought the option. Your loss is limited to the premium paid.

short.definition: You sold the option and collected the premium. You owe the payout if it finishes in the money.

pnl.definition: Profit or loss if you closed the position at current prices. It isn't locked in until you close.

realized-pnl.definition: Profit or loss that's locked in because the position was closed or rolled.

skew.definition: The difference in implied volatility between 25-delta puts and calls. Negative skew means downside protection costs more than upside.

pc-ratio.definition: Open interest in puts divided by calls. Above 1 suggests more hedging or bearish positioning.

roll.definition: Close a position and open a new one at a different strike or expiry in one step, usually to extend a trade.

paper.definition: Simulated fills against Zenith's paper backend. Nothing settles on-chain and no real funds move.

practice.definition: Walk through the full trade flow without sending anything, even to the paper backend. Confirming shows what would have happened.
